lesson.title: Beyond the Sequence: How Cells Remember Which Genes to Use
lesson.summary: Epigenetic regulation refers to heritable changes in gene expression that occur without any change to the underlying DNA sequence, allowing genetically identical cells to become, and remain, different cell types.
lesson.body:
Here is a puzzle: nearly every cell in your body carries the exact same genome, yet a neuron looks and behaves nothing like a liver cell, and a liver cell that divides produces more liver cells, never neurons. Transcription factors, enhancers, and silencers explain how a gene's activity can be turned up or down at any given moment, but they do not by themselves explain why a cell's identity is so stable, generation after generation of cell division. That stability comes from epigenetic regulation.

Epigenetic literally means above or on top of the genetic sequence. Epigenetic regulation refers to changes in gene expression that are heritable, meaning they get passed on through cell division and sometimes even between generations of an organism, but that do not involve any change to the actual DNA sequence, the A's, T's, G's, and C's stay exactly the same. Instead, chemical marks are placed either directly on the DNA molecule or on the histone proteins that package it, and those marks change how accessible a gene is to the transcription machinery without altering the genetic code itself.

The major mechanisms that create these heritable marks, each covered in more depth in the sections that follow, include DNA methylation, chemical tags added directly to DNA bases, histone modification, chemical tags added to the proteins DNA wraps around, and chromatin remodeling, the physical repositioning of that packaging. Small regulatory RNA molecules, such as microRNAs, also contribute to silencing gene expression, though they act after a gene has already been transcribed rather than by marking the DNA or chromatin itself.

Epigenetic regulation matters enormously in practice. It is the reason cells that share a genome can commit to and maintain distinct identities during development. It underlies phenomena like X-chromosome inactivation, where one of the two X chromosomes in a female mammalian cell is stably silenced, and genomic imprinting, where a gene's expression depends on which parent it was inherited from. Because these marks can, in some cases, be influenced by environment or age and are not perfectly permanent, errors or shifts in epigenetic marks are also implicated in diseases such as cancer. Think of epigenetic regulation as an additional, longer-lasting layer of control sitting on top of the transcription factor and enhancer-silencer system already covered: the same genome, running different, stably inherited programs depending on which marks are present.
